ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description first: The circuit diagram is a common-emitter transistor amplifier. The emitter of VT is connected to ground, the collector is connected upward through RC to +VG, and the collector node is coupled through capacitor C2 to the output/load branch RL to ground. Since the emitter is grounded, VCE is the collector-to-ground voltage. Reasoning: The calculated collector current is IC = 1 mA, so the expected voltage drop across RC is 1 mA × 2 kΩ = 2 V. With VG = 12 V, the expected VCE is 12 V - 2 V = 10 V. However, the measured VCE is 8 V, so the voltage drop across RC is 12 V - 8 V = 4 V, giving an actual RC current of 4 V / 2 kΩ = 2 mA. This is 1 mA more than the calculated transistor collector current. The extra DC current must be leaving the collector node through another path. In the shown circuit, C2 should block DC, so a DC path from the collector through RL to ground exists only if C2 is shorted.

method.method_draft: First identify from the image that VCE is the collector-to-ground voltage and that the only normal DC path from +VG through RC is through the transistor collector-emitter path. From the text, the expected IC is 1 mA, so the expected drop on RC is 1 mA × 2 kΩ = 2 V, giving expected VCE = 12 V - 2 V = 10 V. The measured VCE is only 8 V, so the RC current is (12 V - 8 V)/2 kΩ = 2 mA. Since the transistor collector current was calculated as 1 mA, an extra 1 mA must be flowing from the collector node into some other DC path. In the image, that extra path can be through C2 into RL to ground only if C2 is shorted. Therefore the indicated fault is a C2 short circuit.
